extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato/ancient philosophy; scholars of classics and literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for poetry, imitation, and character-portraiture drawn from Plato (as discussed in commentary). Emphasises how imitation affects truth, the educative usefulness of poets, the hierarchy of pleasures, and psychological types (e.g., the tyrant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation about poetry (poetry as outrage on understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: All poetry is an outrage on the understanding, unless the hearers have that balm of knowledge which heals error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should be judged by its potential to mislead; Plato's injunction treats poetry as dangerous unless the audience possesses sufficient knowledge to correct errors. The commentary emphasises this claim and its implications for censorship/regulation of poetry in the ideal state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as thrice-removed imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter is an imitator 'thrice removed' from the truth: there is the idea (bed), the carpenter's bed (copy), and the painter's image (copy of a copy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate representational art by its degree of removal from Forms/truth. The passage stresses the ontological inferiority of imitative art (painter < craftsman < idea) and warns that imitators can deceive children or simple people by representing only appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience knowledge necessary to mitigate poetry's harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is tolerable only 'unless the hearers have that balm of knowledge which heals error.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or presenting poetry, consider the audience's capacity for critical understanding: the same poem may be harmless for a knowledgeable audience but misleading or corrupting for an uneducated one. This is a criterion for whether imitation should be permitted or how it should be framed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness of poets as educators
rubrics_metrics.description: Can the poet be shown to have instructed cities, given laws, advised in war, or produced a way of life named after him? If not, he is only an imitator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poets by their educative and practical contribution: Plato (via the commentator) interrogates Homer — if poets do not provide actionable guidance in polity, war, or crafts, their status as moral/educational authorities is doubtful. Use this to assess claims that art educates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of pleasures (reason > ambition > money)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three kinds of pleasure corresponding to three elements of the soul—reason, passion, desire—and 'the pleasure of the rational part of the soul ... is the pleasantest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting characters or evaluating lives, weigh which class of pleasure predominates: pleasures of reason are truest and more enduring; ambitions and wealth-seeking are lower. Use experience and knowledge as tests for which pleasures are more genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is more than absence of pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is something more than the absence of pain; there are pleasures which have no antecedent pains (e.g. pleasures of smell, hope, anticipation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic portrayals that equate pleasure merely with relief from pain. Represent pleasures that arise positively (anticipation, intellectual joy), and be cautious of the contrast-illusion that makes transient sensual pleasures appear intensely real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation of the tyrannical soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The tyrannical man is dominated by appetites (love like drunkenness/madness), lives amid revelries and harlotries, squanders resources, resorts to force or fraud, becomes a thief or informer, is treacherous, unjust, enslaved to passions and therefore miserable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these behavioural and psychological markers to depict or recognise a tyrannical character: inner slavery (best part subdued), chronic fear and flattery, readiness to harm kin/state for appetite, social isolation, and ultimate misery. The passage provides concrete vices and actions as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of happiness by self-mastery and freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The best and justest man (the royal/master-of-himself) is the happiest; the unjust man is 'the greatest tyrant of himself' and therefore miserable. The individual's freedom/slavery mirrors the state's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral and narrative outcomes by internal freedom (self-mastery) rather than external fortune. In characterization and moral argument, privilege self-rule of reason as the criterion of true happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of numerical and geometrical symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato employs numbers (e.g., 3,4,5; 216; 5040; 729) and geometric relations (Pythagorean triangle, cubes, squares) as symbols of political orders, harmonies, and moral intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using symbolic devices, numbers and geometric figures can encode harmony/order (musical ratios, Pythagorean references) or dramatise moral distances (e.g., the cube 729 as hyperbolic measure between king and tyrant). The commentator warns that Plato treats such arithmetical formulas seriously as philosophical metaphor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soul imagery for moral psychology (beast, lion, man)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form an image of the soul as a 'multitudinous beast' with many heads, a lion, and a man joined together and covered with human skin; the maintainer of justice strengthens the man and restrains the beasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use composite imagery to represent inner psychological parts: the many-headed beast (base desires), the lion (spirited element), and the man (reason/god in man). A noble soul subordinates beast to man; depiction should show nurturing/restraining relations among parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational aim: cultivate self-control and higher principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Our intention in educating the young is to give them self-control; the law desires to nurse up in them a higher principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In portraying education, law, and upbringing, emphasize formation of self-control and alignment with higher principles rather than mere skill-acquisition. This provides a normative criterion for pedagogical depiction and social policy in fiction or theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of handicraft arts' social role
rubrics_metrics.description: The real disgrace of handicraft arts is that those engaged in them have to flatter, instead of mastering their desires; therefore they should be placed under the control of the better principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing social classes or occupations, note Plato's ambivalence: craftsmen are not degraded for their work per se but for social dispositions (flattery, lack of self-rule). Use this to inform class portrayals and the argument for moral cultivation over status-shaming.
